edges.description: The radiolucent lesion is the radiographic appearance of cortex that failed to form: fibro-osseous tissue occupies the subperiosteal cortical bone the affected progenitors did not build.
Reduced cortical stiffness is what the fracture happens through, which is why fracture is an event of the growing tibia rather than of trauma alone.
The lesion is what hurts when the disease is symptomatic, though a large minority of lesions are painless and found incidentally.
Healing across the fracture is delayed and may fail outright, leaving an established pseudarthrosis.

nodes.description: The functional consequence. Forced exon exclusion retards osteoblastic differentiation and inhibits bone-matrix mineralization in vitro, and METΔJMD expression inhibits osteogenic differentiation of skeletal progenitor cells. MET's role here is bidirectional: deleting Met instead enhances osteogenic differentiation of periosteal progenitors.

nodes.description: A targeted treatment, and a direct consequence of recognising OFD as a skeletal RASopathy. MEK inhibition restored osteogenic differentiation in MetΔJMD mouse progenitors and in pseudarthrosis-derived cells from patients, and mirdametinib achieved union in a child with three years of persistent pseudarthrosis. This is a single treated patient with preclinical support, not a trial result.

nodes.description: The causal lesion. Mutations abolish splice inclusion of MET exon 14, so the translated receptor lacks the cytoplasmic juxtamembrane domain. nodes.description: The juxtamembrane domain carries the signal for ubiquitin-mediated degradation. Without it the receptor escapes turnover, accumulates, and acquires a ligand-dependent gain of function. A somatic exon 14 mutation in unilateral disease substitutes a tyrosine residue critical for receptor turnover and has the same stabilising effect, which is what ties the two variant origins to one mechanism.
